pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–7 years

- **Topic:** Living, Dead & Never Alive

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'):** 'explore and compare the differences between things that are living, dead, and things that have never been alive.'

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE):** the living / dead / never-alive three-way distinction is UK-led; the nearest US anchor is the K-2 expectation that all living things have needs (K-LS1-1) and the crosscutting idea of Structure & Function. Note the divergence honestly — NGSS has no dedicated 'once alive vs never alive' performance expectation.

- **Operational details:** Children sort real or pictured objects into THREE groups — living, dead (once alive), and never alive — and justify each placement with observable life-process evidence (grows, feeds, moves by itself, reproduces, senses, breathes). The load-bearing distinction is the middle category: things that were once part of a living thing (a wooden spoon, leather shoe, seashell, dry leaf) are 'dead / once-alive', NOT 'never alive'. Keep the seven life processes as an informal 'test' rather than a memorised list.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, observational sorting). Success is not just correct bins but a life-process REASON — 'the log was a tree so it was alive once' — and correctly resisting the movement=alive shortcut (a car moves but is never alive; a tree is alive but stays put).
bestPractices: Use REAL objects and a THREE-way sort, not two-way — the never-alive vs dead/once-alive split is where the learning happens.
Elicit and directly confront the 'movement = alive' misconception with counter-examples (a car moves but isn't alive; a tree is alive but doesn't move about).
Require a reason grounded in life processes for every placement, not just the label.
Include manufactured items made from once-living material (wooden spoon, paper, cotton, leather, wool) so 'dead / once-alive' is understood as material history.
Contrast a living plant with a plastic plant and a cut/dead flower to attack the 'plants aren't alive' error.
Keep vocabulary light (alive, dead, never alive) but always tie the decision to observable evidence.
keyRepresentations: Three-bin sorting mat (living / dead / never alive) with object-or-picture cards.
A life-processes 'test' checklist (moves by itself, feeds, grows, reproduces, senses, breathes) run against each item.
Same-material origin pairs: living tree → wooden chair; growing flower → pressed dead flower; sheep → wool jumper.
A 'was it EVER alive?' decision fork separating never-alive from once-alive-now-dead.
commonMisconceptions: 'If it moves, it's alive' — sun, fire, cars, rivers, wind judged living.
'Plants aren't alive' — because they don't move about or have faces.
Conflating 'dead' with 'never alive' — treating a rock as 'dead' when it was never alive.
Manufactured items from living material (wood, paper, wool, leather) judged 'never alive'.
'Alive means an animal' — excluding plants, seeds and eggs.
Still or dormant living things (seeds, eggs, a sleeping animal) judged non-living because they aren't moving.

learn.summary: For 6–7 year olds (UK KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'), teach the three-way distinction between living, dead (once alive), and never alive. The load-bearing idea is the middle category: objects made from once-living material (wooden spoon, leather shoe, seashell, dry leaf, wool jumper) were once part of a living thing and so are 'dead / once alive', not 'never alive'. Children sort real or pictured objects into the three groups and justify every placement with observable life-process evidence (grows, feeds, moves by itself, reproduces, senses, breathes) rather than the movement=alive shortcut. Confront directly that a car moves but was never alive, and that a plant is alive even though it stays put.

activities.title: Three-way sort of real objects with a life-process reason
feedback: If a wooden chair or spoon goes into 'never alive', ask where the wood came from and follow it back to a tree; a hidden detail like tree-rings can reveal 'I was a tree — once alive'.

If fire, a car, the sun or a river goes into 'living', run the life-process test together: none of them can sense things, and none came from a parent living thing. Fire and cars do use fuel and air, which can look like feeding and breathing, and fire can spread, but burning or an engine running is not a living body carrying out life processes. Moving or spreading is not enough to be alive.

If the daffodil goes into 'never alive' because 'it can't move about', reground on the full set of life processes (grows, needs water and light, makes new plants); showing a plant growing and slowly turning toward light shows that plants are alive and can move parts of themselves, even though they stay in one place.
If a fallen leaf is called 'never alive', ask where it was yesterday and whether it was alive on the tree — dead means it was once alive but its life processes have stopped, whatever its movement.
Praise reasons that cite a life process or origin from a living thing, not just the correct bin.
activities.rationale: The statutory objective is to explore and compare living, dead, and never-alive things and justify the comparison. Using real objects and requiring a life-process or origin reason (not just a label) targets the hard middle category and the known movement=alive misconception directly.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats' statutory: 'explore and compare the differences between things that are living, dead, and things that have never been alive.'

Young children commonly judge things as alive by movement (classing sun, fire, cars, rivers as living) and often deny that plants are alive; the once-alive vs never-alive distinction is a known difficulty.
learnerActions: Lay out real objects or clear picture cards, for example a potted daffodil, a wooden spoon, a pebble, and a brown leaf that has fallen off a tree.
Sort each object into one of three groups: living now, dead (was once alive), never alive.

For every placement, run a short life-process 'test' aloud — does it grow? feed? make babies/seeds? move by itself? sense? breathe? — and give a reason, e.g. 'the log was a tree so it was alive once' or 'the rock was never part of anything living'.
Include manufactured items made from once-living material (paper, cotton, leather, wool, wood) and trace each back to its source: spoon → plank → tree; jumper → wool → sheep.
Compare a living plant with a plastic plant and a cut/dead flower to decide which is alive, which was once alive, and which never was.
activities.intendedInsight: Dead and never-alive differ by material history: a dead object (or one made from once-living material) was part of a living thing, while a never-alive object never had life processes at all. Being alive is judged by life processes and origin, not by whether something moves about.

activities.title: 'Was it ever alive?' origin reveal gallery
feedback: If a child simply reads the revealed answer, prompt them to restate it as a reason: 'so the jumper was once alive because the wool came from a living sheep'.
Use the never-alive contrast (rock, metal key, plastic) to check that 'never alive' is reserved for things with no living origin.
This reveal is a scaffold: because the child reads the origin rather than deciding and defending it, follow it with the sort activity where they make and justify the call themselves.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or flip-the-flap origin story anchors the once-alive idea as a concrete reference and makes material history memorable, which supports but does not replace independent sorting and justification.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly judge things as alive by movement (classing sun, fire, cars, rivers as living) and often deny that plants are alive; the once-alive vs never-alive distinction is a known difficulty.
learnerActions: Before revealing an answer, predict for each object whether it is living now, was once alive, or was never alive, and say why.
Reveal a short 'was I ever alive?' life-story for each object: chair → tree, wool jumper → sheep, pressed flower → growing flower, pebble → 'never part of a living thing'.
Pair same-origin items so the material history is explicit: living tree → wooden chair; growing flower → pressed dead flower; sheep → wool jumper.
After each reveal, state out loud which of the three groups it belongs in and the life-process or origin reason.
activities.intendedInsight: Many everyday manufactured objects carry a life history — their material was once part of a living thing — so they belong in 'dead / once alive', while truly never-alive things like rocks and metal never had that history.

activities.title: Spot the 'it moves so it's alive' trap
feedback: If a seed or egg is judged non-living because it isn't moving, ask what it could do if planted or kept warm. A healthy seed, or an egg with a chick growing inside, is alive now, with slow life processes going on inside even though nothing moves. (A shop-bought egg will not hatch, so that kind of egg is a less clear example.)

If the sun, fire or a river is judged living, run the life-process test and note that none of them can sense things or came from a parent living thing. Fire uses fuel and air and can spread, which can look like feeding, breathing and making new fires, but burning is not a living body carrying out life processes.
Reinforce that the correct answer to the 'once alive' question is the wooden spoon, because wood came from a living tree; the plastic fork and metal key were never alive.
activities.rationale: A focused recognition task carrying the classic fire/car/sun distractors surfaces the movement=alive misconception efficiently and checks whether the once-living-material idea transfers. Recognition checks discrimination but does not by itself elicit independent construction of a reason, so pair it with the sort.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly judge things as alive by movement (classing sun, fire, cars, rivers as living) and often deny that plants are alive; the once-alive vs never-alive distinction is a known difficulty.
learnerActions: Answer: 'Which of these was once alive — a wooden spoon, a plastic fork, or a metal key?' and explain how you decided.
Sort a short mixed set (sun, fire, car, river, tree, seed, egg, sleeping animal) into living / dead / never alive, saying why for each.
Explain why a car moves but is never alive, and why a tree is alive even though it stays put.
Decide whether a dry seed, an egg, or a sleeping animal is living, and say what each could do.
activities.intendedInsight: Movement does not decide life. Still or resting living things (a healthy seed, an egg with a chick growing inside, a sleeping animal) are alive; moving or spreading non-living things (cars, rivers, fire) are not.

activities.title: Interview the object (optional role-play)
feedback: Keep the dialogue tightly scoped to origin and life processes so it does not drift into fantasy that contradicts the evidence.
Finish by having the child give the classification reason themselves, since the content is finite and the goal is their justification, not the character's.
activities.rationale: A persona/dialogue framing can motivate reluctant reasoners, though the material is limited and the same ideas can be delivered through an authored reveal; offered as an optional alternative with a stated motivational purpose.
learnerActions: Ask an object in role: 'Were you ever alive? Where did you come from?' and let it answer about its origin and life processes.
Keep questions tied to origin (e.g. spoon came from a tree) and the life-process test, then classify the object into one of the three groups.
After the role-play, restate the classification and reason without the persona.
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through an object's origin story can make the once-alive distinction vivid and engaging for young children while keeping the reasoning grounded in origin and life processes.

constraints: Use a THREE-way sort, not two-way: the never-alive vs dead/once-alive split is where the learning happens.
Require a reason grounded in life processes or origin for every placement, not just the correct label.
Include manufactured items made from once-living material (wooden spoon, paper, cotton, leather, wool) so 'dead / once alive' is understood as material history.

Keep the life processes as an informal 'test' (grows, feeds, moves by itself, reproduces, senses, breathes) rather than a memorised list; keep vocabulary light (alive, dead, never alive) but always tied to observable evidence.

When countering the movement=alive trap for fire, admit that fire can look as if it grows, 'feeds' on fuel, needs air and starts new fires. Rest the case on what fire lacks: it is not a body made of living parts, it cannot sense, and it does not come from a parent living thing. It is burning, which stops when the fuel or air runs out.
Reveal/flip galleries and role-play are scaffolds: because the child reads or hears the answer rather than deciding and defending it, follow them with independent sorting and justification.
Recognition-only tasks check discrimination but do not elicit a child's own constructed reason; use them alongside, not instead of, the justified sort.

The living/dead/never-alive three-way distinction is UK-led. NGSS has no dedicated 'once alive vs never alive' performance expectation; the nearest US anchors are K-LS1-1 (all living things have needs) and Structure & Function — note the divergence honestly rather than overclaiming alignment.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified; the Open University OpenLearn misconceptions claim is marked unverified in the source row — treat the misconception framing as plausible but not independently confirmed here.

The original recommendation leaned heavily on a single drag-and-drop format and asserted that 3D 'adds no insight' and that dialogue 'adds little'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to format choices with stated affordances and limits.

A dormant seed/egg being 'living' is a defensible simplification at this age (it has the potential and biological organisation for life processes); kept because it supports the anti-movement message, but note the nuance that an inert dry seed (or a shop egg) shows no active life processes.

The original pedagogy refers to the 'seven life processes' but lists only six (grows, feeds, moves by itself, reproduces, senses, breathes); the full MRS GREN convention adds excretion. The count has been resolved to six to match the test actually run, with the seven-process convention noted here only.

Fire is conventionally treated as never alive, but because it spreads and appears to grow, the feedback deliberately avoids resting the counter on growth and uses feeding/breathing/reproduction instead.

probeDeeper: You said the pebble was never alive — what would make you change your mind about it?
Is a dry seed living, even though it isn't doing anything right now? What could it do if you planted it?
Your jumper is made of wool — was the wool ever alive? How do you know?
The leaf was on the tree yesterday. Was it alive then? What about now — what changed?
assess.correctAnswer: Living now: the daffodil (it grows, needs water and light, makes seeds). Once alive, now dead: the fallen leaf AND the wooden spoon (wood was part of a living tree). Never alive: the pebble. The reasoning must appeal to life processes or to having come from a living thing — not to whether the thing moves.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Only things that move are alive, so the plant isn't living' — judges life by movement (animism's flip side); may also call the sun, fire or a river 'alive'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground on the full set of life processes (grows, needs water/light, makes new plants) using the vocabulary prerequisite; show time-lapse of a plant growing and turning to light so movement-free life is visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: The daffodil isn't alive — it can't move around like an animal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places the daffodil in 'never alive' or 'not sure', and justifies with 'it can't move/walk'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The wooden spoon was never alive — it's just a spoon' — does not recognise that once-living materials (wood, wool, leather, paper) came from living things.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the material back to its source ('where does wood come from?') — spoon→plank→tree; contrast with the pebble, which was never part of anything living. Reteach in place; this origin distinction is the heart of this topic.
errorPatterns.distractor: The wooden spoon was never alive — it's just a spoon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts the wooden spoon (or a wool item) into 'never alive' alongside the pebble.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Dead means it stopped working/moving' — restricts 'dead' to things that visibly moved, so a fallen leaf is called 'never alive' rather than dead.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask where the leaf was yesterday and whether it was alive on the tree; establish that dead = was once alive but life processes have stopped, independent of movement.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts the leaf with the pebble in 'never alive', or hesitates because 'a leaf doesn't do anything'.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by movement or present appearance: calls the plant non-living, or the wooden/wool item 'never alive'; cannot give a life-process or origin reason.
responseLevels.full: Sorts all three groups correctly, including the wooden spoon and fallen leaf, justifying each by life processes or origin-from-a-living-thing, and transfers the rule to a fresh case (a seed, a wool jumper).
responseLevels.partial: Correctly places the obvious cases (animal = living, pebble = never alive) and can recite life processes, but slips on the plant or on once-living materials — lists the criteria without applying them to the hard items.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out four things: a potted daffodil, a wooden spoon, a pebble, and a brown leaf that has fallen off a tree. Ask: 'Which of these are living right now? Which were alive once but are dead now? And which have never, ever been alive? Point to each one and tell me how you decided.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two items split the class. The daffodil separates a child who reasons from life processes from one who believes 'only things that move about are alive' (they park the plant in 'never alive'). The wooden spoon separates a child who tracks that wood ORIGINATED in a living tree from one who sorts by present appearance ('it's just a spoon, never alive'). A child can only place both correctly by using the right criterion, and can't place them right by a movement rule.
